quote: Yeah. And I'm interested, but I know they're very expensive. So if if this is gonna be very expensive, you could just take me off the list.
stewart_read: Donna states the classic cost objection before her bill has even been captured. This is a prime spot for the objection-inversion flip (her current situation is the reason to act), but the rep instead gives a generic 'no upfront cost' reassurance.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be deliberately holding the flip until after the bill number is captured, planning to use the actual $300 figure later — but no later flip occurs (03:32), so this reads as a genuine miss rather than a deferred strategic move.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to hold this exact moment and revisit with the bill number once captured — the pieces were both on the table (cost fear at 02:34, bill at 03:19) but never joined.

stewart_read: The bill figure (~$300/month) is captured cleanly, giving the rep the exact number needed to flip Donna's earlier cost objection.
coaching_implication: This capture should be the pivot point back to Donna's 02:34 statement — 'that's exactly the number that makes solar worth a look' — but the rep instead just validates and moves to the next verify item.

quote: But yeah. No. 300 is kind of expensive, but we can definitely help get that cut down for you. I mean, I don't blame you for wanting to find an alternative.
stewart_read: This is the natural flip point: bill captured, cost anxiety already on record. The rep acknowledges the bill is 'kind of expensive' but the response is validation, not inversion — the bill is never explicitly reframed as the reason to act rather than a reason to hesitate.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep could be pacing the call to avoid sounding pushy given Donna's earlier 'take me off the list' comment — a soft-touch strategic choice. But since no flip appears anywhere later in the call either, this reads as an omission rather than a deliberate soft approach.
coaching_implication: Show the rep this exact clip: bill number + prior objection were both already on the table. The flip line was available and unused — practice turning 'that's expensive' into 'that's exactly why this is worth 30 minutes.'

quote: And have you ever looked into solar before?
stewart_read: Donna discloses a prior solar inquiry from roughly ten years ago that she abandoned over cost. The rep acknowledges the technology has improved but never probes which company, what she was quoted, or why exactly she dropped it — competitive intel a closer would want.
coaching_implication: Coach a simple follow-up habit: 'do you remember which company that was with, or what the quote looked like?' costs 15 seconds and gives the closer real context on her price anchor.

quote: But everything looks good on my end. So the only thing I'll need from you, Donna, is just a copy of your kilowatt usage.
stewart_read: Rep transitions straight into bill-collection logistics without creating any curiosity about what her specific design or savings might look like, despite having just captured her bill and cost history.
coaching_implication: A single line tying her $300 bill to 'let's see exactly what that could look like for your home' before pivoting to bill collection would create pull rather than just procedural compliance.

quote: Okay. That would be great. K. Awesome. I I sent that already. So, you should have my info, and then we will keep in touch.
stewart_read: The call ends with a bill-collection text promise but no appointment day/time, no one-hour block statement, no handshake — the entire button-up sequence is absent.
alternative_hypothesis: Because the bill wasn't available (customer away from home until Monday), the rep may be strategically deferring appointment-setting until the bill is in hand. But even so, a specific callback time ('I'll call you Monday at 2pm') was available and not used — Donna herself proposed 'Monday' and the rep didn't lock it.
coaching_implication: Even when the bill can't be collected live, the rep should still lock a specific callback day/time rather than leaving it as 'we will keep in touch' — this is the procedural fragility the schema flags as unanchored_soft_exit.

quote: I'll I'll I'll hear from you on Monday. Right? Give me a call on Monday if you if you get a chance.
stewart_read: Donna proactively offers a timeframe ('Monday') for the rep to call her back, essentially handing the rep the booking opportunity, but the rep's response treats it as optional rather than locking a specific time.
coaching_implication: When the customer hands you a day, convert it immediately: 'Great, let's say Monday at 10am — does that work?' instead of leaving it loose.

quote: Yeah. If I don't get if I don't call you because sometimes I forget. I get busy with stuff. So just give me a call, and I'll try and I'll pull that up, and I'll see if I can make a copy of it for you.
stewart_read: The rep openly admits unreliability ('sometimes I forget') and shifts the burden of follow-through onto the customer, which undermines legitimacy and leaves the appointment entirely unowned.
coaching_implication: This line should never be said aloud to a customer — flag directly with the rep. Admitting forgetfulness erodes trust and guarantees a soft, ownerless close.
